title: Kaomoji Face Badge
pitch: An 8x8 LED face that switches expressions with a button: happy, wink, love, angry, sleepy and shocked.

guide.about: Each face is 8 rows of 8 bits (1 = LED on). You'll design pixel art as binary numbers, and the MAX7219 chip does all the LED work for you.
parts: or a power bank to wear it
wiring: other leg to GND (touch pad: SIG → Pin 2, set USE_TOUCH true)
steps: Install the LedControl library.
Wire the matrix (the input side, marked DIN): VCC 5V, GND, DIN 12, CS 10, CLK 11.
Wire the button between Pin 2 and GND.
Upload. The face blinks now and then by itself!
Press the button to change expression.
guide.test: Each press shows the next face. Every few seconds the current face blinks. If faces look upside down, set FLIP to true.
next: Design your own faces: draw them on graph paper, then convert each row to binary.
Chain 4 matrices for scrolling text.

title: Snake on 8x8
pitch: The classic snake game on a glowing LED matrix, steered with a thumb joystick.

guide.about: The snake is a list of coordinates. Each step adds a new head and drops the tail, unless you just ate. A classic lesson in arrays and game loops.
steps: Install LedControl.
Wire the matrix (DIN 12, CS 10, CLK 11) and joystick (VRx A0, VRy A1, SW 2).
(Optional) Buzzer through 220Ω on Pin 8.
Upload and push the stick to start moving.
guide.test: The snake moves every 300 ms and speeds up as it grows. Eat the blinking dot to grow. Hit yourself and the score scrolls in the Serial Monitor (9600). Click the stick to restart.
next: Let the snake wrap around the edges.
Show the score on a TM1637.

title: Pocket Lab Pet
pitch: A tiny virtual pet lives on your OLED. Feed it, play with it, let it sleep, or it gets grumpy (>_<)!

guide.about: Meet Bitty, your pocket lab pet. Hunger, fun and energy slowly drop over time; two buttons pick and perform actions. You'll learn timers, simple stats and drawing faces.
steps: Install Adafruit SSD1306 and Adafruit GFX Library.
Wire the OLED (5V, GND, SDA A4, SCL A5) and the two buttons (pins 2 and 3 to GND).
Upload. Bitty hatches!
SELECT cycles Feed → Play → Sleep. DO performs the action.
Keep all three bars above zero to keep Bitty happy.
guide.test: Bars shrink over time; Bitty's face changes from (^_^) to (-_-) to (>_<). Feeding fills hunger, Play fills fun (but costs energy), Sleep restores energy.
next: Add an age counter and evolution stages.
Save the stats in EEPROM so Bitty survives power-off.

title: Space Dodge
pitch: Pilot a tiny ship with a joystick and dodge falling asteroids. The longer you survive, the faster they come!

guide.about: An arcade game: joystick input, falling objects in an array, collision checks and difficulty that ramps up.
steps: Install Adafruit SSD1306 and Adafruit GFX Library.
Wire the OLED to 5V, GND, A4, A5.
Wire the joystick: VRx A0, VRy A1, SW Pin 2.
Upload and click the stick to launch.
guide.test: Your ship moves in all directions; asteroids fall from the top. Survive as long as possible: the score is your time. Crash = big explosion and GAME OVER.
next: Add a shield power-up.
Add stars in the background for a parallax effect.

title: Desert Runner (LCD game)
pitch: A running game on a 16x2 text LCD using custom pixel characters. Jump the cacti!

guide.about: Text LCDs let you design up to 8 custom 5x8-pixel characters. Here they become a running character (2 animation frames) and a cactus.
steps: Install the LiquidCrystal I2C library.
Wire the LCD (GND, 5V, SDA A4, SCL A5) and the button on Pin 2.
Upload. If the screen is blank, adjust the blue contrast screw or change the address to 0x3F.
Press the button to start and to jump.
guide.test: The runner animates on the bottom row while cacti scroll in from the right. Jumping lifts it to the top row for a moment. The score shows top-right.
next: Add birds on the top row that you must NOT jump into.
Store the high score in EEPROM.

title: Fortune Oracle
pitch: Ask a question, shake the box, and the oracle reveals your fate on the LCD. Very mysterious. Much wow.

guide.about: The accelerometer notices a shake (a big change in acceleration). Then a random fortune appears with a dramatic reveal. The fortunes are stored in flash memory (PROGMEM) to save RAM.
parts: a small one, inside a box
or a power bank inside the box
steps: Install LiquidCrystal I2C.
Wire both modules to 5V and GND, both SDAs to A4 and both SCLs to A5.
Upload. The screen says "Ask, then shake…".
Ask a yes/no question out loud, then shake the breadboard (gently!).
Build it into a box with the LCD showing through a window.
guide.test: A shake shows "The spirits speak..." then a random answer like "Yes, definitely!" or "The stars say: maybe".
next: Add your own fortunes and inside jokes.
Add a buzzer for a spooky reveal sound.

title: Pomodoro Study Timer
pitch: 25 minutes of focus, 5 minutes of break, with a progress bar and a gentle chime. Homework, conquered.

guide.about: The Pomodoro technique: focus for 25 minutes, then rest 5. The LCD shows a countdown and a bar made of custom characters; one button starts, pauses and resets.
steps: Install LiquidCrystal I2C.
Wire the LCD, the button (Pin 2) and the buzzer (Pin 8 via 220Ω).
Upload.
Tap to start/pause. Hold for 2 seconds to reset.
guide.test: FOCUS counts down from 25:00 with a filling bar. At zero a chime plays and BREAK 05:00 starts. Rounds are counted on the screen.
next: Change FOCUS_MIN and BREAK_MIN to suit you.
Add a long break after 4 rounds.

title: Pocket Calculator
pitch: A working calculator: keypad in, LCD out. A=+, B=−, C=×, D=÷, #==, *=clear.

guide.about: Read numbers digit by digit, remember the operator, and calculate when # is pressed. It even handles chained sums like 2+3×4 (left to right, like a basic calculator).
steps: Install Keypad and LiquidCrystal I2C.
Connect the keypad's 8 pins: 1–4 to pins 9, 8, 7, 6 and 5–8 to pins 5, 4, 3, 2.
Wire the LCD to 5V, GND, A4 and A5.
Upload and calculate: 12 A 30 # shows 42.
guide.test: Top line shows what you type, bottom line shows the result. Dividing by zero shows "Error".
next: Add a decimal point key (re-label one of A–D).
Add memory keys.

title: TV Remote Color Lamp
pitch: Use any infrared remote, even your old TV one, to change an RGB lamp's color from the couch.

guide.about: Every remote button sends a code of infrared flashes. This sketch works with any NEC-style remote: each new button press switches to the next color, and the Serial Monitor shows each button's code so you can assign your own.
wiring: module pins are labeled; bare receivers: check the datasheet order
through 220Ω (not 3 or 11: the IR library uses that timer)
steps: Install the IRremote library (by shirriff, z3t0, ArminJo).
Wire the IR receiver: OUT to Pin 2, + to 5V, − to GND.
Wire the RGB LED (long leg to GND) with 220Ω resistors: red 9, green 10, blue 6.
Upload and open the Serial Monitor at 9600.
Point the remote at the receiver and press any button.
guide.test: Each button press (holding doesn't repeat) changes the color: red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, blue, purple, pink, white, off. The code of each button prints, e.g. "Button code: 0x45".
next: Map specific buttons to specific colors using the printed codes.
Control a servo or a relay with the remote instead.

title: Bluetooth Lamp (Android)
pitch: Send 0–9 from a phone app over Bluetooth to set a lamp's brightness. Android phones and PCs only.

guide.about: The HC-05 is a wireless serial cable. Whatever the phone app sends arrives at the board like typed text. Note: iPhones can't use classic Bluetooth serial. On iPhone use the Wi-Fi lamp idea with an ESP32 instead.
steps: Wire the HC-05: VCC 5V, GND, TXD to Pin 10.
Build the voltage divider: Pin 11 → 1kΩ → HC-05 RXD, and 2kΩ from HC-05 RXD to GND.
Add the LED with 220Ω on Pin 9.
Upload. The HC-05's LED blinks fast (waiting to pair).
On an Android phone, pair with "HC-05" (PIN 1234 or 0000), install a free app like "Serial Bluetooth Terminal", connect, and send 0–9.
guide.test: Sending 9 = full brightness, 5 = half, 0 = off. The board replies "Brightness: 50%" back to the app.
next: Send r/g/b letters to control an RGB LED.
Build a Bluetooth robot car with the L298N.

title: Wireless Joystick Link
pitch: Two boards, two radios: tilt a joystick on one and a servo moves on the other, up to ~50 m away.

guide.about: nRF24L01+ radios send small packets of data between boards. One sketch does both jobs: set ROLE to TRANSMITTER for the joystick board and RECEIVER for the servo board. If the signal is lost, the servo returns to center (a "failsafe").
parts: or a power bank for one of them
wiring: long leg (+) to VCC, right at the module
steps: Install RF24 (by TMRh20) and Servo.
On BOTH boards wire the nRF24 exactly as in the table, with a 10µF capacitor across its power pins.
Transmitter board: add the joystick. Set ROLE to TRANSMITTER and upload.
Receiver board: add the servo on Pin 6. Set ROLE to RECEIVER and upload.
Power both boards and move the joystick.
guide.test: The servo follows the joystick's X axis with almost no delay. Unplug the transmitter: after 1 second the servo centers itself. The receiver's Serial Monitor (9600) shows the packets.
safety: nRF24 modules must be powered from 3.3V. On Nano clones the 3.3V pin is often too weak; that's why this guide uses Uno boards.
next: Send both axes to a pan-tilt mount.
Turn it into a remote control for the robot car.

title: SD Weather Logger
pitch: Records temperature and humidity with a timestamp every minute onto a microSD card. Open it in Excel later!

guide.about: Data logging is real science: the board writes one line of CSV (comma-separated values) per minute, which spreadsheets open directly. The RTC gives each line a real date and time.
parts: or a USB charger for long logging
steps: Format the microSD card as FAT32 on your PC.
Install DHT sensor library, Adafruit Unified Sensor, RTClib and SD.
Wire everything as in the table (SPI for the SD card, I2C for the clock).
Upload. The clock takes your PC's time if it hasn't been set yet.
Let it run. Later, unplug, take out the card and open LOG.CSV on your PC.
guide.test: The Serial Monitor (9600) prints each saved line, like "2026-11-05 14:32,24.1,48.0". The file grows by one line per minute.
safety: Always unplug power before removing the SD card, or the file may get damaged.
next: Add a BMP280 (with a 3.3V supply) for pressure.
Make a chart in Excel or Google Sheets.

title: Tea & Coffee Thermometer
pitch: Dip the waterproof probe in your drink: it shows the temperature and beeps when it's cooled to the perfect sip.

guide.about: The DS18B20 talks over a single data wire (1-Wire). The code watches the temperature fall and beeps once when it reaches about 60°C, a comfortable drinking temperature for most people.
steps: Install OneWire, DallasTemperature and TM1637.
Wire the probe (red 5V, black GND, yellow Pin 2) and the 4.7kΩ resistor from Pin 2 to 5V.
Wire the TM1637 to 5V, GND, CLK 3, DIO 4.
Upload. Wash the probe, then dip it in your hot drink.
guide.test: The display shows the temperature like "72°C". When the drink cools below 60°C after being hotter than 65°C, it beeps three times.
safety: Only the metal probe goes into the drink. Keep the wires' plastic end and the electronics dry.
Wash the probe before and after use.
next: Change DRINK_C to your favorite temperature.
Use two probes to compare two cups.

title: Anime Sound Board
pitch: Three buttons, three of your favorite sound clips or voice lines, played loud through a real speaker.

guide.about: The DFPlayer Mini plays MP3 files from a microSD card and drives a speaker by itself. The board just sends commands like "play track 2" over serial.
parts: one 1kΩ for the DFPlayer RX line
wiring: protects the 3.3V RX pin and removes hiss
never connect the speaker to GND
steps: Put your sound files on the microSD card in a folder named mp3, named 0001.mp3, 0002.mp3, 0003.mp3.
Install the DFRobotDFPlayerMini library.
Wire the DFPlayer exactly as in the table (don't forget the 1kΩ on RX).
Connect the speaker to SPK_1 and SPK_2.
Wire the three buttons to pins 2, 3, 4 and the optional pot to A0.
Upload and press a button!
guide.test: Each button plays its own clip; pressing again restarts it. The Serial Monitor (9600) says "DFPlayer ready". If it says it failed, check the card and the TX/RX wires.
safety: Only use sound clips you made yourself or are allowed to use.
Start with a low volume: small speakers distort when too loud.
next: Add more buttons (the DFPlayer supports thousands of files).
Combine with the PIR alarm to play a voice line when someone enters.

title: Neon Ring Clock
pitch: A glowing analog clock made of 16 LEDs: pink hour hand, cyan minutes, a twinkling yellow seconds dot.

guide.about: Map hours, minutes and seconds onto 16 LED positions around a ring, and blend colors where hands overlap. The DS3231 keeps time even when unplugged.
steps: Solder wires to the ring's 5V, GND and DIN pads.
Install Adafruit NeoPixel and RTClib.
Wire the ring (DIN through 330Ω to Pin 6) and the DS3231 (A4/A5).
Upload: the clock takes your PC's time the first time.
Place LED 0 at the top (12 o'clock). If the hands run backwards, set REVERSED to true.
guide.test: Pink marks the hour, cyan the minutes, and a yellow dot steps around for seconds. Brightness is kept low for a calm night glow.
safety: Soldering: hot iron, use the stand and ventilate.
next: Add hourly rainbow animations.
Add a light sensor to dim it at night.
